solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Low budget gardens with chain fencing

indicators.note: a fence runs all the way round a plot, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: a chain of things in a row is a string of them
the verb: a gardener hoes the beds

explanation.surface: A cheap garden made affordable by fencing it off with nothing more than a chain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gardens' reads as a noun, plots of land, but it is the verb: to garden is to work the soil with a hoe.
explanation.definitionFit: Done on a shoestring is an idiom for managing with very little money, so the word itself serves as an adjective for cheap.

clue.text: Way to make a revolution constitutional

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
a roll is one turn over

explanation.surface: How to bring about a revolution by legal, constitutional means.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constitutional' poses as the political adjective; here it is the old noun for a walk taken for one's health.
explanation.definitionFit: A constitutional is a gentle walk taken for health, and a leisurely walk is exactly that kind of outing.

clue.text: Lots of dogs but no lead

indicators.note: the lead is what goes in front, so without it the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: poodles are a breed of dog

explanation.surface: A crowd of dogs being walked, not one of them on a lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' sits naturally with dogs as the leash; cryptically it is the leading letter, the P.
explanation.definitionFit: Oodles is informal for a great quantity, a plentiful amount, the same as lots.

clue.text: Music producers apply pressure over hits

parts.note: to squeeze is to press hard
to box someone is to hit them, as in boxing their ears

explanation.surface: Record producers leaning on the people behind the chart hits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Music producers' suggests people in a studio; here it means instruments that produce music. In a down entry, 'over' simply puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A squeeze-box is an informal name for an accordion or concertina, instruments that make music when squeezed.

clue.text: Part of some petrol engines

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the words that follow are taken, a run from inside them

parts.note: the letters run consecutively across the join of these two words

explanation.surface: A component found in certain petrol engines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part' looks like a mechanical component to go with the engines; it is the definition, as in a part in a play, and the answer straddles petROL Engines.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor's part in a play or film is their role, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Critic in a novel finally said some corrosive stuff

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are made into something new

parts.note: taken as written, letters to be rearranged

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of the word it qualifies, its closing letter

parts.note: the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A reviewer who, in a book, ends up making acid, cutting remarks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' reads as the noun, a book the critic appears in, but it is the adjective new and signals the rearrangement. 'Corrosive' also suggests a scathing review.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitric acid is a strong mineral acid that eats through metals, so it is an example of a corrosive substance.

clue.text: Time off insufficient for study

indicators.note: when something is off it has been taken away, so a letter is removed

parts.note: scant means barely enough
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A student complaining that the time off allowed is too short to revise properly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time off' looks like a holiday; it is T taken off the end of SCANT.
explanation.definitionFit: To scan is to examine closely, look over carefully, which is one sense of study as a verb.

clue.text: Verse cut by priest left unfinished

indicators.note: something left unfinished is missing its end, so the final letter goes
by means beside; read as a passive, the agent named after this word comes first in the answer

parts.note: a cleric is a member of the clergy
to hew is to chop or cut

explanation.surface: A poem cut short by a priest who never finished it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left unfinished' looks like it describes the verse; it applies to the priest. Read 'cut by priest' as passive: the priest does the cutting, so he leads.
explanation.definitionFit: A clerihew is a four-line comic verse form about a famous person, invented by E. C. Bentley.

clue.text: Preferring your own stuffed pimentos

indicators.note: stuffed food has been filled and mashed about, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone who prefers to stuff their own peppers rather than buy them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuffed pimentos' reads as a dish, olives or peppers with filling; 'stuffed' is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Nepotism is favouritism shown to relatives, giving jobs and advantages to family members over outsiders.

clue.text: Island set, out to lunch on wine and fish

indicators.note: in an across entry, A on B puts B first, so what precedes this word is sent to the back

parts.note: red wine, called simply red

indicators.note: out to lunch is slang for crazy, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: Mull is an island in the Scottish Inner Hebrides
taken as written, letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An island holiday: a table set, everyone out at lunch over wine and fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out to lunch' sounds like a meal to go with wine and fish, but it is slang for crazy. Mull is a Scottish island.
explanation.definitionFit: Red mullet is a prized Mediterranean food species with reddish skin, a kind of sea fish.

clue.text: Go with Jack to reverse vehicle

indicators.note: reversing means going backwards, so the letters are read from the end

parts.note: to go, informally, is to urinate
J is the abbreviation for jack in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: Instructions for a learner driver: go with Jack to practise reversing the car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go' looks like setting off, but it is the euphemism for a toilet trip.
explanation.definitionFit: A jeep is a small rugged four-wheel-drive motor car, first built for the US army.

clue.text: At the Sorbonne, it's the done thing

parts.note: surface reading: what polite society expects, correct etiquette
setter's reading: put the phrase into French, the language of the Paris university, and translate thing done word for word

explanation.surface: Etiquette among the students and lecturers of a Paris university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The done thing' means proper conduct in English; rendered literally into French, a thing done becomes a phrase English has borrowed. The Sorbonne is the famous university in Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: A fait accompli is something already done and settled before others can object, literally an accomplished fact.

clue.text: Acoustic No 1 songs

indicators.note: acoustic concerns sound, so the word is taken by how it is heard

parts.note: number one is the one in front, the head

explanation.surface: Unplugged versions of chart-topping songs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Acoustic' suggests unplugged guitars to go with chart hits; it is the sound signal. LEADER and LIEDER are pronounced the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Lieder are German art songs, typically for solo voice and piano, as written by Schubert or Schumann.

clue.text: Great film about a partner in crime

indicators.note: about means around, so the outer letters are placed round something

parts.note: great in size
taken as written
a thin film of moisture or haze

explanation.surface: A great crime film about an accomplice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great film' sounds like a review, but the two words join as one outer piece. 'Partner in crime' usually means accomplice; here the partnering itself is the crime.
explanation.definitionFit: A bigamist marries while still married, so becoming someone's spouse is itself an offence in law.

clue.text: Triggering a single tax in effect

indicators.note: in places one set of letters inside another

parts.note: to put into effect is to put into action
a single one is I, the Roman numeral
value added tax, the UK sales tax

explanation.surface: A flat tax coming into force, triggered by new legislation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In effect' reads as 'in practice', but 'in' is the insertion signal. VAT, value added tax, is the British sales tax.
explanation.definitionFit: Activation is the act of setting something going, starting a device or process, which is what triggering it does.

clue.text: Entrance by the Queen, backed by ship's siren

parts.note: the verb, to put under a spell

indicators.note: something backed has gone backwards, so its letters run the other way

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina
SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: The Queen arrives by sea while a ship's siren sounds behind her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrance' reads as an arrival, but it is the verb en-TRANCE, to bewitch. 'Siren' poses as a ship's horn; it is the temptress of legend.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth a siren lured sailors with song; in general use she is a seductive, bewitching woman.

clue.text: Cushions of cloth at the back, like on footwear

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only its closing letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word
as and like both mean in the manner of
socks are worn on the feet

explanation.surface: Cushioning made of fabric at the heel, as in a padded shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, 'on' simply puts AS above SOCKS, the order the clue gives them.
explanation.definitionFit: Hassocks are firm padded cushions for kneeling on in church, or footstools, so they are a type of cushion.

clue.text: Take on quiet, more mature university dons

parts.note: the call for hush

indicators.note: to don is to put on clothing, so one piece wears another, wrapping it

parts.note: comparative of old
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Quiet, older academics at a university taking on new responsibilities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dons' looks like university lecturers to go with 'university'; it is the verb, puts on, so OLDER wraps U.
explanation.definitionFit: To shoulder a burden is to accept it, bearing the responsibility, the same as taking it on.

clue.text: One encouraging the other

parts.note: surface reading: a person giving someone else support and encouragement
setter's reading: a coy British euphemism for sex, so the thing is one that stimulates desire

explanation.walkthrough: 'The other' seems to mean the second of two people; in British slang a bit of the other is sex, so this is something that encourages lovemaking.
explanation.definitionFit: An aphrodisiac is a food or drug said to arouse sexual desire, named after Aphrodite, goddess of love.

clue.text: Glassware on a lab bench or counter

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a long-necked glass vessel used for distilling
second meaning: a sharp reply, or to answer back

explanation.surface: Where to put the chemistry glassware: on the lab bench or the counter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Counter' sits naturally beside a bench as another work surface; it is the verb or noun for a quick reply.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a bulb-shaped laboratory distilling flask and also a witty comeback made in reply.

clue.text: Tale handed down on purpose

parts.note: in cricket the on side of the field is also called the leg side
an end is an aim, as in ends and means

explanation.surface: A story passed down through the generations, told deliberately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On purpose' reads as 'deliberately'; split, 'on' is the cricket term for the leg side (the half of the field behind the batter's legs) and 'purpose' an end.
explanation.definitionFit: A legend is a traditional story passed from generation to generation, popularly believed but unverified.

clue.text: Vessel of gold, church vault secures

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so one piece holds the others

parts.note: a vault spans a space, arching over it
Au is the chemical symbol for gold
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A golden chalice locked away in the church vault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vault' suggests a strongroom; it is the verb, to arch across. 'Vessel of gold' suggests a chalice, but only 'Vessel' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A saucepan is a deep cooking pot with a handle, and a vessel is any container for liquids.

clue.text: Salt on spinach

parts.note: surface reading: seasoning sprinkled over a dish of greens
setter's reading: an old salt is a sailor, and this one runs on spinach, his famous strength food

explanation.walkthrough: 'Salt' is the condiment in the kitchen reading; in crosswords it is a seasoned sailor, and the cartoon sailor man gains his strength from cans of spinach.
explanation.definitionFit: Popeye is the cartoon sailor created by E. C. Segar, whose muscles swell when he eats spinach.

clue.text: Stuff used up making brandy

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the pulp of skins and pips left after grapes are pressed
second meaning: a spirit distilled from that leftover pulp

explanation.surface: Leftovers from winemaking being turned into brandy.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is true: the spent grape pulp is distilled into a brandy of the same name, so the link word is literally accurate.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the refuse of pressed grapes and the French spirit distilled from it, like Italian grappa.

clue.text: Guiding principles about fondue, regularly ignored

parts.note: C is short for circa, about

indicators.note: ignoring letters at regular intervals means every other one is dropped, keeping the rest

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Etiquette for fondue parties being routinely disregarded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning'; it is C for circa. The odd letters of 'fondue' are the ones ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: A code is a set of rules or standards of conduct, as in a code of practice, a body of guiding principles.

clue.text: Reject fool for opening seedy club

indicators.note: opening something up lets other letters be put inside it

parts.note: a dive is a disreputable bar or nightclub
a sap is a gullible person
pro means in favour of

explanation.surface: A bouncer refusing entry to a fool hoping to open a seedy nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' looks like a link word, but it gives letters. 'Opening' seems to be the start of a club; it is the verb, prising the club open.
explanation.definitionFit: To disapprove is to judge something unacceptable and refuse to sanction it, which matches reject as a verb.

clue.text: Active agent safeguarding resistance

indicators.note: safeguarding something means keeping it protected, wrapped inside

parts.note: a secret agent is a spy
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A spy in the field protecting the resistance movement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resistance' suggests a wartime underground; it is the physics symbol R.
explanation.definitionFit: Spry describes someone, usually elderly, who is lively and nimble, energetic in movement.

clue.text: Direct plays with puns ad-libbed

indicators.note: to play with something is to fiddle with it, so the letters are moved around

parts.note: taken as written, letters to be rearranged
taken as written, letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A theatre director staging comedies full of improvised wordplay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Direct plays' reads as an instruction to stage drama; 'Direct' is fodder and 'plays' the verb that scrambles it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ad-libbed is improvised on the spot rather than written beforehand, with no prepared text to follow.
